implementation_notes: In Kotlin coroutines the one-shot latch is structured concurrency: coroutineScope already joins every child before it returns, and awaitAll()/joinAll() await a set of Deferred/Job values without blocking a thread - awaitAll fails immediately when any deferred fails, unlike a sequential map { it.await() }. An explicit rendezvous is expressed with a rendezvous Channel (capacity RENDEZVOUS), whose send suspends until a receiver arrives, or with one Channel per phase that the last arriver closes. Because the JVM primitives are JVM-only, this is also the only realization for multiplatform code.
pitfalls: awaitAll fails promptly on the first failure, but neither awaitAll nor a sequential await cancels work launched outside the calling scope: children of a supervisorScope or of another CoroutineScope must be cancelled explicitly.
A coroutineScope waits for every child, so a child that never completes hangs the parent - the same liveness hazard as a barrier, with no timeout unless withTimeout wraps the scope.

Blocking primitives (CountDownLatch.await, Thread.join, runBlocking) inside a coroutine block the carrier thread and can exhaust Dispatchers.Default; use join/await and keep blocking calls in Dispatchers.IO.

variants.name: JVM primitives: CyclicBarrier / CountDownLatch / Phaser
variants.idiom_name: java.util.concurrent CyclicBarrier, CountDownLatch and Phaser on the JVM
variants.implementation_notes: On the JVM, Kotlin uses exactly the Java primitives - CyclicBarrier for reusable phases (with an optional action run by the last arriver), CountDownLatch for one-shot fan-in, Phaser for dynamic parties - and the language adds only thin sugar, such as a lambda for the barrier action. This is the realization for code that runs on real platform threads and blocking work, because it is the only variant that offers a reusable barrier and per-phase aggregation; coroutine-based code should prefer the awaitAll variant, since every call here blocks the carrier thread.
pitfalls: JVM-only: Kotlin/Native and Kotlin/JS have no java.util.concurrent, so commonMain cannot reference CyclicBarrier or CountDownLatch at all.

The CyclicBarrier action runs in the last arriving thread; if it throws, the barrier breaks and every waiter receives BrokenBarrierException, so catch and abort with a clear error rather than retrying.
Blocking waits inside coroutines starve the dispatcher: wrap them in withContext(Dispatchers.IO) or switch to the suspend equivalents (join/await).
